title: Style
intro: Joue avec le style de l'anglais : mettre l'emphase comme un écrivain, passer du familier au formel, parler comme un vrai Canadien et déjouer les mots-pièges.

boss.name: Lord Register
boss.taunt: Greetings, jeune personne. Je passe de « What's up? » à « I am writing to inform you » en un battement de cils. Never have I lost a duel… et ce n'est pas aujourd'hui que ça va commencer !
boss.defeat: Never have I been so humiliated… Bon. Fair enough, eh ?

units.title: L'emphase
units.goal: Mettre l'emphase sur une idée avec l'inversion, les phrases clivées et le do d'insistance.

lesson.text: En français, pour frapper fort, tu dis : « Jamais je n'ai vu une chose pareille ! » L'anglais soutenu fait pareil, mais avec un truc spécial : quand la phrase **commence par un mot négatif ou restrictif**, on **inverse** l'auxiliaire et le sujet, comme dans une question : [[Never have I seen such a mess!]]

lesson.title: L'inversion après un mot négatif
lesson.text: Mot négatif + **auxiliaire** + **sujet** + verbe. S'il y a déjà un auxiliaire (have, had, should, is…), on le met devant le sujet : [[Never have I been so tired.]] S'il n'y en a pas (présent ou passé simple), on ajoute **do / does / did** et le verbe revient à la **base** : [[Rarely does she complain.]] [[Little did he know…]]

head: Début de phrase
Sens
Exemple
rows: [[Rarely do we see moose in the city.]]
[[Not only did she win, but she also broke the record.]]
[[Hardly had I sat down when the phone rang.]]
[[No sooner had we arrived than it started to rain.]]
Under no circumstances / At no time
en aucun cas / à aucun moment
[[Under no circumstances should you open this door.]]
[[Little did they know what was coming.]]
Only then / Only when / Only after
c'est seulement alors / quand / après que

lesson.title: Les phrases clivées
lesson.text: Pour mettre une partie de la phrase sous le projecteur : [[It was Tom who broke the window.]] (C'est Tom qui…) ou [[What I need is a long nap.]] (Ce dont j'ai besoin, c'est…). Avec **What**, le verbe be est au **singulier** : [[What we need is more time.]] On dit aussi [[All I want is…]] (Tout ce que je veux, c'est…). Pour une personne, c'est [[who]] (ou [[that]]), jamais [[which]] ni [[what]].

lesson.title: Le do d'insistance
lesson.text: Pour insister ou contredire quelqu'un, ajoute **do / does / did** devant le verbe à la base, et appuie dessus en parlant : [[I do like your drawing!]] (Je l'aime vraiment !) [[She does know the answer.]] [[I did finish my homework!]] (Je te jure que je l'ai fini !)

items.en: Never have I eaten such a big poutine.
items.fr: Jamais je n'ai mangé une aussi grosse poutine.

items.en: Only when the bell rang did we stop working.
items.fr: C'est seulement quand la cloche a sonné qu'on a arrêté de travailler.

items.en: It was Mei who found the solution.
items.fr: C'est Mei qui a trouvé la solution.

items.en: What surprised me was the silence.
items.fr: Ce qui m'a surpris, c'est le silence.

items.en: I did call you, but you didn't answer!
items.fr: Je t'ai appelé, je te jure, mais tu n'as pas répondu !

lesson.text: Piège de francophone : on ne garde **pas** l'ordre normal après [[Never]] en début de phrase : ~~Never I have seen~~ → [[Never have I seen]]. Après l'auxiliaire, le verbe reste à la base : ~~Little did he knew~~ → [[Little did he know]]. Avec **Only when / Only after**, l'inversion se fait dans la **deuxième** partie : [[Only when I got home did I notice]]. Et retiens les couples : **Hardly… when**, mais **No sooner… than**.

lines.en: I know! Not only did she stop every penalty, but she also scored the last one.

lines.en: Yes! Little did the other team know that she used to play forward.

lines.en: What I don't understand is why the coach didn't try that earlier.

lines.en: Only at the last minute did he think of it.
lines.fr: C'est seulement à la dernière minute qu'il y a pensé.

lines.en: Well, I do hope she plays in the final!
lines.fr: Eh bien, j'espère vraiment qu'elle va jouer en finale !

grammar.q: Never ___ such a delicious poutine.
grammar.explain: Never en début de phrase → inversion : auxiliaire (have) + sujet (I) + participe (eaten).

grammar.q: Not only ___ the dishes, but he also cleaned his room.
grammar.explain: Après Not only en début de phrase, on inverse avec did : did he wash (verbe à la base).

grammar.q: No sooner had we sat down ___ the movie started.
grammar.explain: On dit No sooner… than. (C'est Hardly qui va avec when.)

grammar.q: Hardly had she closed the door ___ someone knocked.
grammar.explain: On dit Hardly… when. (C'est No sooner qui va avec than.)

grammar.q: Only when I got home ___ that my phone was missing.
grammar.explain: Avec Only when, l'inversion se fait dans la deuxième partie de la phrase : did I notice.

grammar.q: It was Malik ___ scored the winning goal.
grammar.explain: Dans une phrase clivée sur une personne : It was Malik who… (ou that). Jamais which ni what pour une personne.

grammar.q: Never ___ so much snow in one day!
grammar.explain: Never en tête → inversion : have I seen.

grammar.q: Little ___ that his friends were planning a surprise.
grammar.explain: Little en tête → did + sujet + verbe à la base : did he know.

grammar.q: Under no circumstances ___ leave the room during the exam.
grammar.explain: Under no circumstances en tête → inversion : should you.

grammar.q: Rarely ___ late for school.
grammar.explain: Rarely en tête → on inverse be et le sujet : is Ethan.

grammar.q: What I love about winter ___ skating on the canal.
grammar.explain: Phrase clivée avec What : le verbe be est au singulier → is.

grammar.q: You say I never help, but I ___ the dishes yesterday!
grammar.explain: Do d'insistance au passé : did + verbe à la base → I did do the dishes.

grammar.q: Never have I saw such a mess.
grammar.explain: Après have, il faut le participe passé : have I seen, pas saw.

grammar.q: No sooner had we arrived when it began to snow.
grammar.explain: No sooner va toujours avec than.

grammar.q: Not only did she sang, but she also danced.
grammar.explain: Après did, le verbe revient à la base : did she sing.

grammar.q: It was Amir which helped me with my project.
grammar.explain: Amir est une personne : It was Amir who (ou that) helped me.

grammar.q: Only after the game did we went for pizza.
grammar.explain: Après did, le verbe est à la base : did we go.

grammar.q: She does likes your idea; she's just shy.
grammar.explain: Do d'insistance : does + verbe à la base → she does like.

reading.title: The Night the Lights Went Out
reading.text:
Never had Priya been so excited about a sleepover. Her cousin Léa had come all the way from Montreal, and the two girls had planned the perfect evening: pizza, a movie and a board game that would probably last until midnight.

Little did they know that the weather had other plans. Around eight o'clock, freezing rain began to fall on Ottawa. Hardly had the movie started when the lights flickered and the screen went black. The whole street was dark.

What surprised Priya most was how quiet the house became. No fridge humming, no music from her brother's room, nothing at all. Only then did she realize how much noise their machines made every day.

Her dad lit a few candles and found an old lantern in the basement. Not only did he find the board game in the dark, but he also managed to make hot chocolate on the gas stove. Under no circumstances, he told the girls, were they to open the fridge, because the food had to stay cold.

It was Léa who suggested telling stories instead of playing. At first, Priya rolled her eyes. Rarely did her cousin have good ideas, or so she thought. But Léa's story about a lost beaver who dreamed of becoming a hockey player was so funny that even Priya's dad laughed until he cried.

No sooner had they finished the third story than the lights came back on. The fridge started humming, the movie started playing again, and Priya's brother cheered from upstairs.

Strangely, nobody wanted to watch the movie anymore. “Can we turn the lights off again?” Léa asked. And she did mean it.

The next morning, Priya wrote one sentence in her diary: “Never have I enjoyed a blackout so much.”

questions.q: Why was Léa at Priya's house?
choices: Her own house had lost power.
She had come from Montreal for a sleepover.
She wanted to borrow a board game.

questions.q: What happened just after the movie started?
Why did Priya's dad tell the girls not to open the fridge?
choices: He was hiding a surprise in it.
It was making too much noise.
He wanted to keep the food cold.

questions.q: Before that night, what did Priya think of Léa's ideas?
choices: She thought they were usually excellent.
She thought they were usually not very good.
She thought they were too scary.
She had never heard any of them.

questions.q: Why did nobody want to watch the movie anymore?
choices: It was too late to watch anything.
They had enjoyed the evening without electricity more.

questions.q: What does the last sentence of the story suggest?
choices: The blackout became a happy memory for Priya.
Priya was angry about the blackout.
Priya was scared during the whole night.
Priya wants to stop writing in her diary.

units.title: Formel ou familier
units.goal: Passer du langage familier au langage formel et écrire un courriel poli et soutenu.

lesson.text: Un même message peut s'habiller en jogging ou en complet-cravate. À ton ami : [[I need help.]] À la directrice : [[I would appreciate your assistance.]] C'est ce qu'on appelle le **registre** : familier, neutre ou formel.

lesson.title: Le courriel formel, étape par étape
lesson.text: 1. Ouverture : [[Dear Sir or Madam,]] (si tu ne connais pas le nom). 2. Le but : [[I am writing to request information about…]] 3. La demande polie : [[I would be grateful if you could…]] 4. Une pièce jointe : [[Please find attached…]] 5. La fin : [[Thank you in advance for your assistance.]] [[I look forward to hearing from you.]] 6. La signature : [[Kind regards,]] ou [[Sincerely,]]. **Pas de contractions** dans un courriel formel : [[I am]], pas [[I'm]].

lesson.title: look forward to + -ing
lesson.text: Dans [[look forward to]], le mot [[to]] est une **préposition**, pas le « to » de l'infinitif. Donc il est suivi d'un nom ou d'un verbe en **-ing** : [[I look forward to hearing from you.]] [[We look forward to meeting you.]] Jamais ~~look forward to hear~~.

lesson.title: L'oral familier : gonna, wanna, gotta
lesson.text: Entre amis, à l'oral ou par texto : [[gonna]] = going to, [[wanna]] = want to, [[gotta]] = (have) got to. [[I'm gonna be late.]] [[Do you wanna come?]] [[I gotta go!]] Attention : [[gonna]] remplace seulement **going to + verbe**. Pour un lieu, on garde [[going to]] : [[I'm going to the mall]], jamais ~~I'm gonna the mall~~. Et ces formes n'ont **jamais** leur place dans un courriel formel.

items.en: I am writing to request information about your summer camp.
items.fr: Je vous écris pour demander des renseignements sur votre camp d'été.

items.en: I would be grateful if you could reply by Friday.
items.fr: Je vous serais reconnaissant de répondre d'ici vendredi.

items.en: Please find attached my application form.
items.fr: Vous trouverez ci-joint mon formulaire d'inscription.

items.en: We apologize for any inconvenience.
items.fr: Nous nous excusons pour tout désagrément.

items.en: I'm gonna call you after supper.
items.fr: Je vais t'appeler après le souper.

lesson.text: Deux pièges de francophone : 1) ~~I look forward to see you~~ → [[I look forward to seeing you]]. 2) Le faux ami [[demand]] ne veut **pas** dire « demander » : il veut dire **exiger**, et ça sonne agressif ! Pour demander poliment, c'est [[request]] ou [[ask for]].

grammar.q: Quelle phrase convient le mieux dans un courriel à ta directrice d'école ?
choices: Hey! I wanna talk about the field trip.
Dear Madam, I am writing regarding the field trip.
Yo, what's up with the field trip?
Hi! Gotta ask you something about the field trip.
grammar.explain: Formule d'ouverture formelle (Dear Madam), pas de contraction, et regarding au lieu de about.

grammar.q: I look forward to ___ you at the meeting.
grammar.explain: Dans look forward to, to est une préposition : on met le verbe en -ing.

grammar.q: Quelle est la version formelle de : « Can you tell me when the gym opens? »
choices: Could you inform me when the gym opens?
Can you tell me when does the gym open?
Tell me when the gym opens.
Wanna tell me when the gym opens?
grammar.explain: Could (plus poli que can) + inform (formel pour tell). La 2e phrase a en plus une erreur : pas d'inversion dans une question indirecte.

grammar.q: I'm ___ be late, sorry!
grammar.explain: I'm gonna = I'm going to. I'm wanna et I'm gotta n'existent pas, et I'm going be oublie le to.

grammar.q: Quelle formule termine bien un courriel formel ?
grammar.explain: Kind regards (ou Sincerely) est la formule de fin polie. Les autres sont pour les amis ou la famille.

grammar.q: Dans un courriel, le verbe anglais « demand » veut dire…
grammar.explain: Faux ami ! demand = exiger (agressif). Pour demander poliment : request ou ask for.

grammar.q: We ___ more chairs for the concert.
grammar.explain: need → require dans un registre formel.

grammar.q: I am writing to ___ information about your summer jobs.
grammar.explain: request information = demander des renseignements (formel). Jamais demand !

grammar.q: Please ___ the book to the library by Friday.
grammar.explain: give back → return en registre formel.

grammar.q: I look forward to ___ from you.
grammar.explain: look forward to + -ing : hearing.

grammar.q: We would like to ___ you that the meeting has been cancelled.
grammar.explain: tell someone → inform someone en registre formel.

grammar.q: Sorry, I ___ go, my mom is calling me!
grammar.explain: À l'oral entre amis, have got to → gotta.

grammar.q: I look forward to meet you next week.
grammar.explain: look forward to + -ing : meeting, pas meet.

grammar.q: I would be grateful if you could sending me a brochure.
grammar.explain: Après could, le verbe est à la base : could send.

grammar.q: I am writing to demand information about the swimming lessons.
grammar.explain: demand = exiger, c'est agressif ! Pour demander poliment des renseignements : request.

grammar.q: I'm gonna the mall with my cousins.
grammar.explain: gonna remplace seulement going to + verbe. Pour un lieu : I'm going to the mall.

grammar.q: We look forward to welcome you at the museum.
grammar.explain: look forward to + -ing : welcoming.

reading.title: Two Messages, Two Styles
reading.text:
Jaden wanted to volunteer at the Riverside Community Centre this summer. First, he texted his best friend, Malik.

“Hey! Gonna apply for that volunteer thing at the centre. Wanna do it with me? Gotta send the email tonight, so let me know!”

Malik answered with a thumbs-up and three exclamation marks. Then Jaden opened his laptop to write to the manager, Sandra Okafor. His first try began with “Hi Sandra, I wanna help at your camp.” He read it aloud, frowned and deleted everything.

His older sister, Ana, was looking over his shoulder. “You're not texting a friend,” she said. “You're writing to someone who might give you a job. Make it sound professional.”

Forty minutes later, this is what Jaden sent:

Dear Sandra Okafor,

I am writing to request information about volunteer positions at the Riverside Community Centre this summer. I am fourteen years old, I speak French and English, and I have assisted at my school's reading club for two years.

I would be grateful if you could inform me whether you require any documents, such as a reference letter. I am available from the end of June until the end of August.

Thank you for your time. I look forward to hearing from you.

Sincerely,
Jaden Moreau

Two days later, he received an answer. The manager thanked him for his clear and polite message and invited him to an interview. At the bottom, she had added a short note: “It is rare to receive such a well-written email from a student.”

Jaden forwarded the message to Malik. A minute later, his phone buzzed: “Wait, you wrote that? Can you write mine too?”

questions.q: Why did Jaden delete his first try?
choices: Malik told him to start again.
It sounded too casual for a message to a manager.
He had written to the wrong person.

questions.q: Which of these did Jaden mention in his email?
choices: His age and the languages he speaks

questions.q: What did Jaden want to know?
choices: Whether he needs to send any documents

questions.q: What can we guess about Ana?
choices: She works at the community centre.
She knows how a formal message should sound.

questions.q: What did the manager think of Jaden's email?
choices: She thought it was impressive for a student.

questions.q: What does Malik's last text suggest?
choices: He is surprised, and he would like help with his own email.
He is angry that Jaden applied without him.
He thinks the email is too formal.

units.title: L'anglais de la vraie vie
units.goal: Comprendre et utiliser l'anglais parlé de tous les jours, version canadienne.

lesson.text: À l'école, on apprend l'anglais « du livre ». Mais dans la cour d'école ou à l'aréna, à Ottawa, tu vas entendre [[no worries]], [[my bad]], [[legit]]… Voici ton kit de survie de l'anglais parlé, version canadienne.

head: Expression
Sens
Exemple
rows: [[Pizza or tacos? It's up to you.]]

lesson.title: Le Canada en mots
lesson.text: [[washroom]] = les toilettes dans un lieu public. [[double-double]] = un café avec deux crèmes et deux sucres. [[loonie]] = la pièce de un dollar (le huard) et [[toonie]] = la pièce de deux dollars. [[toque]] = une tuque. [[pop]] = une boisson gazeuse. [[runners]] = des espadrilles. [[keener]] = un élève super zélé (un peu moqueur). Et le célèbre [[eh]], à la fin d'une phrase, pour demander si l'autre est d'accord : [[Cold today, eh?]]

lesson.title: Un registre familier
lesson.text: Toutes ces expressions sont **familières** : parfaites avec tes amis, ta famille ou à l'aréna, mais à éviter dans un courriel formel (rappelle-toi l'étape 11.2). On écrit [[Thank you for your assistance]] à la directrice, pas [[No worries, you're awesome!]]

items.en: My bad, I forgot to text you back.
items.fr: Ma faute, j'ai oublié de te répondre.

items.en: Do you have a toonie for the parking meter?
items.fr: As-tu une pièce de deux dollars pour le parcomètre ?

items.en: That guy online seems sketchy.
items.fr: Ce gars en ligne a l'air louche.

items.en: Can I take a rain check on the movie?
items.fr: Est-ce qu'on peut remettre le film à plus tard ?

items.en: Nice game, eh?
items.fr: Beau match, hein ?

lesson.text: Pièges : [[pop]] veut dire une boisson gazeuse, pas seulement la musique pop ! [[hang out]] (passer du temps ensemble) n'est **pas** [[hang up]] (raccrocher le téléphone). Et [[my bad]] sert pour une **petite** erreur ; pour quelque chose de grave, dis plutôt [[I'm really sorry]]. Attention aussi à l'orthographe : [[loonie]], pas [[looney]] (qui veut dire « cinglé ») !

Le sais-tu ? La pièce de un dollar canadien montre un **huard** ([[loon]] en anglais) : c'est pour ça qu'on l'appelle [[loonie]]. Quand la pièce de deux dollars est arrivée, les gens ont mélangé [[two]] et [[loonie]] pour inventer [[toonie]] !

lines.en: I'm starving. Wanna grab something before the game?

grammar.q: Ton ami te dit : « Sorry, I stepped on your foot! » Tu réponds gentiment :
grammar.explain: No worries = pas de souci. My bad, c'est ce que dit la personne qui a fait l'erreur.

grammar.q: Tu as pris le crayon de ton amie par erreur. Tu dis : « ___, here it is. »
grammar.explain: My bad = c'est ma faute, oups. On le dit pour une petite erreur qu'on a faite soi-même.

grammar.q: Un inconnu en ligne t'offre des cadeaux gratuits si tu lui donnes ton mot de passe. C'est…
grammar.explain: sketchy = louche, pas fiable. Ne donne jamais ton mot de passe !

grammar.q: Au Canada, un toonie vaut…
grammar.explain: toonie = la pièce de deux dollars (two + loonie). Le loonie vaut un dollar.

grammar.q: « Do you want to come skating? » — « ___ What time? »
grammar.explain: I'm down = je suis partant. C'est la seule réponse qui accepte l'invitation.

grammar.q: Ton amie explique qu'elle ne peut pas venir parce qu'elle a un rendez-vous chez le dentiste. Tu réponds : « ___. Next time, then! »
grammar.explain: Fair enough = c'est correct, je comprends ta raison.

grammar.q: Quel mot n'a PAS sa place dans un courriel formel ?
grammar.explain: awesome est familier. Les trois autres sont des mots formels de l'étape 11.2.

grammar.q: Can you watch my bag? I need to go to the ___.
grammar.explain: Au Canada, les toilettes publiques : the washroom.

grammar.q: Do you want to ___ at my place on Saturday?
grammar.explain: hang out = passer du temps ensemble (pas hang up, qui veut dire raccrocher).

grammar.q: I can't come tonight. Can I take a ___?
grammar.explain: take a rain check = remettre une invitation à plus tard.

grammar.q: Cold today, ___?
grammar.explain: Le fameux eh canadien, à la fin d'une phrase, pour chercher l'accord de l'autre.

grammar.q: Wear your ___, it's minus twenty outside!
grammar.explain: Une tuque = a toque (on voit aussi l'orthographe tuque en anglais canadien).

grammar.q: Pizza or tacos? I don't mind, it's ___ to you.
grammar.explain: It's up to you = c'est toi qui décides.

grammar.q: Can I borrow a looney for the vending machine?
grammar.explain: La pièce de un dollar s'écrit loonie. looney veut dire « cinglé » !

grammar.q: No worry, I'll help you clean up.
grammar.explain: L'expression est toujours au pluriel : No worries.

grammar.q: Do you want to hang up at the park after school?
grammar.explain: hang out = passer du temps ensemble. hang up = raccrocher le téléphone.

grammar.q: It's up for you, we can leave whenever you want.
grammar.explain: L'expression est It's up to you.

reading.title: Karim's First Week
reading.text:
On his first day at his new school in Ottawa, Karim thought his English was pretty good. He had studied it for years in Paris. By lunchtime, however, he wasn't so sure.

In the hallway, a boy bumped into him and said, “My bad!” before running off. Karim had no idea what was bad, or whose it was. At recess, a girl named Chloé asked if he wanted to hang out after school. Karim imagined laundry hanging on a line and politely said no.

Luckily, Chloé didn't give up. She sat next to him at lunch and offered him a cookie. When Karim thanked her, she answered, “No worries!” He wondered what she was supposed to be worried about.

Then she asked if he had a loonie for the vending machine. Karim looked confused, so she showed him a gold-coloured coin with a bird on it. “It's a loon,” she explained. “That's why we call it a loonie. And the two-dollar coin is a toonie.” Karim laughed for the first time that day.

After school, Chloé's dad picked them up. He was holding a coffee. “Double-double,” he said proudly, as if it were a secret password. Karim later learned that it meant two creams and two sugars.

That evening, Karim wrote a list in his notebook: my bad, no worries, hang out, loonie, toonie, double-double. At the bottom, he added one more word that he had heard at least ten times: eh.

The next morning, Chloé waved at him. “Want to hang out at recess?” she asked.

“I'm down,” Karim answered with a grin.

Chloé raised her eyebrows. “Wow, you learn fast, eh?”

questions.q: Why did Karim say no when Chloé first invited him?
choices: He had to go home early.
He didn't understand what “hang out” meant.

questions.q: Why is the one-dollar coin called a loonie?
choices: Because it was designed in Paris.
Because it is used in vending machines.

questions.q: What does “double-double” mean in the story?
choices: A coffee with two creams and two sugars

questions.q: How did Karim most likely feel during his first morning?
choices: Confused by the English he heard

questions.q: Why does Chloé raise her eyebrows at the end?
choices: She is angry that Karim is late.
She is surprised that Karim used a slang expression so naturally.
She thinks Karim is being rude.

questions.q: What did Karim write in his notebook?
choices: A letter to his friends in Paris

units.title: Les mots qui piègent
units.goal: Ne plus confondre les paires de mots anglais qui se ressemblent ou se prononcent pareil.

lesson.text: Même les anglophones se trompent avec ces mots-là ! Ils se ressemblent, se prononcent parfois pareil… mais ne veulent pas du tout dire la même chose. Un bon détective des mots les repère tout de suite.

head: Paire
La différence
Exemple
rows: [[The noise affects me. It has a bad effect on me.]]
[[Don't lose your keys! My shoe is loose.]]
[[Can I borrow your pen? Can you lend me your pen?]]
dire quelque chose / dire à quelqu'un
[[She said hello. She told me a secret.]]
monter tout seul / lever quelque chose
moins de (qu'on compte) / moins de (qu'on ne compte pas)
[[good advice; I advise you to rest]]
[[taller than me; and then we left]]

lesson.title: Les sosies à apostrophe
lesson.text: [[its]] = son, sa (possessif) / [[it's]] = it is ou it has. [[their]] = leur / [[there]] = là / [[they're]] = they are. [[your]] = ton, ta / [[you're]] = you are. [[whose]] = à qui, dont / [[who's]] = who is ou who has. Truc infaillible : si tu peux remplacer par **it is / they are / you are / who is**, mets l'apostrophe. Sinon, pas d'apostrophe !

lesson.title: Le casse-tête lie / lay
lesson.text: [[lie]] (s'allonger) : lie, **lay**, lain, lying. [[lay]] (poser quelque chose à plat) : lay, **laid**, laid, laying. Le piège : le passé de lie est… [[lay]] ! [[Yesterday I lay on the couch.]] mais [[Yesterday I laid my bag on the floor.]] (Et [[lie]] au sens de mentir est régulier : lie, lied, lied.)

lesson.text: Pièges de francophone : ~~Can you borrow me your pen?~~ → [[Can you lend me your pen?]] On **emprunte à** quelqu'un ([[borrow from]]) et on **prête à** quelqu'un ([[lend to]]). Aussi : [[advice]] est indénombrable : ~~an advice, advices~~ → [[some advice, a piece of advice]]. Et ~~She said me~~ → [[She told me]] : [[tell]] veut une personne juste après.

Truc de mémoire : stationEry, avec un **e** comme **e**nveloppe (papeterie). StationAry, avec un **a** comme **a**rrêté (immobile). Et le [[principal]] de ton école est ton **pal** (copain, en anglais)… enfin, on l'espère !

grammar.q: I have hockey ___ tonight.
grammar.explain: Ici c'est un nom (l'entraînement) : practice avec un c. Au Canada, practise avec un s, c'est le verbe.

grammar.q: The new rule will ___ everyone in the school.
grammar.explain: Il faut un verbe (influencer) : affect. effect est le nom.

grammar.q: My jeans are too ___; I need a belt.
grammar.explain: loose = lâche, trop grand. lose = perdre.

grammar.q: There were ___ people at the game than last week.
grammar.explain: people se compte (un pluriel) : fewer.

grammar.q: When the teacher came in, everyone ___ from their seats.
grammar.explain: On se lève tout seul : rise, rose, risen. raise a besoin d'un objet (raise your hand).

grammar.q: Yesterday I was so tired that I ___ on the couch all afternoon.
grammar.explain: S'allonger = lie, et son passé est lay. laid est le passé de lay (poser quelque chose).

grammar.q: My parents ___ me to study harder.
grammar.explain: Le verbe s'écrit avec un s : advise → advised. advice (avec un c) est le nom.

grammar.q: Please ___ your hand if you know the answer.
grammar.explain: On lève quelque chose (la main) : raise.

grammar.q: This sandwich costs ___ than the pizza.
grammar.explain: costs less = coûte moins cher. fewer va seulement devant un nom pluriel qu'on peut compter.

grammar.q: ___ backpack is this? It's on my chair.
grammar.explain: À qui = whose. who's = who is.

grammar.q: My brother is taller ___ me.
grammar.explain: Pour comparer : than. then veut dire ensuite.

grammar.q: The students forgot ___ notebooks at home.
grammar.explain: Possessif (leurs) : their.

grammar.q: Can you borrow me your eraser, please?
grammar.explain: Prêter = lend. borrow veut dire emprunter.

grammar.q: The dog wagged it's tail happily.
grammar.explain: Possessif (sa queue) : its, sans apostrophe. it's = it is.

grammar.q: There were less cars on the road this morning.
grammar.explain: cars se compte : fewer cars.

grammar.q: I need your advise on my essay.
grammar.explain: Ici c'est le nom (ton conseil) : advice, avec un c.

grammar.q: Please be quite during the test.
grammar.explain: Silencieux = quiet. quite veut dire assez.

grammar.q: She said me the truth.
grammar.explain: tell + personne : She told me the truth. (say ne prend pas la personne directement.)

reading.title: Ask Priya, the Word Detective
reading.text:
Every week, our school newspaper receives letters from students who are confused about English words. This week, Priya answers two of them.

Dear Priya,
My older brother says I should never borrow his headphones without asking. So last week, I asked him, “Can you borrow me your headphones?” He laughed so hard that he couldn't answer. What did I do wrong?
Embarrassed in Orleans

Dear Embarrassed,
Don't worry, it's a very common mistake for French speakers! You borrow something from someone, but someone lends something to you. So next time, try: “Can you lend me your headphones?” or “Can I borrow your headphones?” Your brother will have fewer reasons to laugh, and you'll have more music.

Dear Priya,
My teacher circled “its” and “it's” in red on my essay about my dog. I thought they were the same word! She also says that “I laid down after the walk” is wrong. My dog lies down all the time. Why can't I?
Confused in Kanata

Dear Confused,
You can, of course! But the verb is tricky. When you rest your body, you lie down, and in the past, you lay down. When you put an object somewhere, you lay it down, and in the past, you laid it. So: “I lay down after the walk,” but “I laid my keys on the table.”

As for its and it's, here is my secret: if you can say “it is” or “it has,” use the apostrophe. “It's a sunny day.” If not, it shows possession: “My dog loves its blanket.”

Remember, these mistakes don't affect how smart you are. Even adults make them! But fixing them will have a great effect on your writing.

Keep the letters coming!
Priya

questions.q: Why did the brother laugh so hard?
choices: The writer used “borrow” where “lend” was needed.
He didn't want to share his headphones.
He was listening to a funny podcast.

choices: The team lost it's first game.

questions.q: What does Priya mean when she says the brother “will have fewer reasons to laugh”?
choices: The brother will stop telling jokes.
If the writer uses the right word, there will be no mistake to laugh at.

questions.q: What is Priya's attitude toward the students who write to her?

She is annoyed by their questions.
She thinks their teachers are wrong.

questions.q: Why does Priya say that even adults make these mistakes?
choices: To prove that English is impossible
To explain why the teacher is wrong
To show that the mistakes are normal and not a sign of being less smart
